Jennie Livingston's documentary about New York City's 1980s ballroom scene and the Black and Latino queer people who built its houses, competitions, and performance styles.
The film was released in 1990 and selected for the U.S. National Film Registry in 2016 for preservation.

Its interviews and footage document ballroom participants' accounts of family, gender, race, class, and aspiration. The film's authorship and representation have also prompted debate about a white filmmaker documenting a community of color and about who receives recognition and economic benefit.
The film is an important source for understanding ballroom culture, but it is one documentary made from a particular perspective, not a complete account of the community.

A shared cache for cargo builds, run as the mbx command. Cargo still resolves dependencies, plans builds, and runs tools; mbx restores matching compiler outputs from one shared store and compiles the rest. No daemon or cache server is needed for local use.
Equivalent compilations share cache keys when checkout paths differ, so building one git worktree warms the next.
The store has a disk budget. Managed target/ directories are collected when their checkout disappears, goes unused, or exceeds its budget. mbx gc --dry-run previews a collection.
Independent Cargo commands share CPU and memory permits and deduplicate identical compilations in flight.

CI can reuse the cache through the GitHub/Action cache, a compatible cache server, or an S3-compatible bucket. jdx/mr-boxington-action sets it up. Pull request builds only read from a cache server or bucket; writes come from pushes to protected branches.
Install with mise (mise use --global --tool-option mr_boxington=true rust mr-boxington), or with cargo install mbx --locked followed by mbx setup.
Builds on ideas from sccache and kache; kache directly inspired its design.
Set the mr_boxington option on the rust tool and add mr-boxington as its own tool. Cargo then runs through mbx under mise exec, mise tasks, activated shells and mise's shims, with no mbx setup step.
Calling a toolchain's cargo directly, such as ~/.cargo/bin/cargo, skips mbx. Check with command -v cargo.
My global mise config turns it on: dotfiles#181.

Acousmatic music is a genre of electroacoustic music that is composed for playback via speakers, rather than being performed live by musicians with visible instruments. The listener engages with the pure sonic experience, unmediated by the visual cues of instrumental performance.
I use this term to refer to when I have a true musical experience. It applies to both making and listening to music.
Describes a scale with no semitones between adjacent steps. From the Greek an- ("without") and hēmitonion ("half tone").
The opposite is hemitonic: a scale with one or more semitone steps.
The word is used mostly to separate the two families of pentatonic scale.
Anhemitonic: Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Major and its modes, including Music/Scale/Pentatonic/Minor.
The word is used mostly to separate the two families of pentatonic scale.
Hemitonic: Music/Scale/Hirajoshi and the other Japanese in-scale pentatonics.
The word is used mostly to separate the two families of pentatonic scale.
Music/Scale/Whole Tone is also anhemitonic. Every seven-note scale in twelve-tone equal temperament is hemitonic.

Bariolage is a string playing technique, primarily used on the Violin (but also on other bowed string instruments), characterized by rapid alternation between notes on adjacent strings—often between a static open string and varying stopped notes on a neighboring string.
Creates a shimmering or pulsating texture.
Common in Baroque and Classical music, notably in J.S. Bach’s solo string works.
Exploits the contrast in tone between open and fingered strings.
Often used to simulate polyphony or to add rhythmic drive.
In Bach’s Partita No. 3 in E major, BWV 1006, the Preludio uses bariolage extensively, alternating between the open E string and notes played on the A string.
From French barioler, meaning "to streak with several colors"—a metaphor for the tonal contrasts produced.

MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party

Twenty-five saved sounds on the Microfreak, grouped by the job each one does at a party: talking voices, slow atmosphere, organ and bells, bass and lead lines, jump scares, and a sung or spoken vocoder. Every preset below is on the device today; a read of the instrument on 2026-10-29 Thu matched the slot names in the garden.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party

The reasons come from each preset's saved settings, read off the device on October 25, 2026 and recorded on its preset page. None of these sounds have been auditioned yet, so the order is a starting point for the next session.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party
The PRESSURE row in each patch responds to key pressure or velocity, depending on the instrument's global Utility setting.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party

The Microfreak/UG/06 Dig Osc/03 Types/11 Speech oscillator comes from the speech research behind the Speak & Spell toy. It produces vowels, numbers, letters and whole words. A toy voice saying words nobody chose is the most direct Halloween sound the instrument makes.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party

Why it fits: a Sample-and-Hold LFO steps the speech formants and also pushes the word selector in the opposite direction, so each step lands on a different syllable. The result is a voice that keeps saying broken fragments, like a possessed toy or a radio between stations.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party
Pressing harder opens the filter almost fully, so you can keep it muffled under the music and make it suddenly clear on one note.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party
How to use it: hold a single low note and let the random syllables run under a pad. Lean on the key when you want the voice to come forward.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party

Why it fits: real number stations are shortwave broadcasts of a voice reading numbers for unknown listeners, and the cold, flat delivery is creepy on its own. This patch uses the Speech oscillator with a filtered Sample-and-Hold LFO on the word selector, so it reads a stream of numbers that changes on its own.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party
Pressure closes the filter a little and raises its resonance, which makes the voice sound more like it is coming through a radio.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party
How to use it: an intro or interlude, alone, before the beat drops. Pair it with Microfreak/Preset/141 Digital Sea for radio static.

MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party

Why it fits: the filter has a fair amount of resonance, and an LFO pulls the cutoff down while it also changes the word, so the voice sounds like it is talking from inside a metal pipe. That reads as a robot or a ghost in the machine.

Pressure speeds up the arpeggiator or sequencer, so a held chord can start chattering faster as you press.
MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party
How to use it: run it through the arpeggiator on a minor chord, then press to make the chatter speed up before a drop.

MicroFreak presets for a Halloween party

Why it fits: each key selects a different word, and the sound has a long decay with no sustain. You can "play" a sentence by choosing keys, which makes it the most controllable of the talking patches. A doll that says a word when you touch it is a good bit for a party.

Pressure brings in the cycling envelope and makes it rise faster, so pressing harder makes the word stutter.

How to use it: find a few keys whose words land well and repeat them as a call-and-response with the crowd.
